As with all things Harry and Meghan-related, their various media forays have spawned copious amounts of reactionary content and commentary. Each appearance, commission and production has been dissected: there have been blockbuster hits, much-publicised misses and some brutal reviews along the way.
![Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, being interviewed on a patio by Oprah Winfrey](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/39e484b95e19012167c9c1a9fc0532eb347b7a20/0_0_3500_2509/master/3500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
For Harry, the pull of returning to the UK, if perhaps not permanently, has been clear for a while.
He says he loves his country, and in an interview with the Guardian last year, he admitted he hankered for home.
“I have always loved the UK and I always will love the UK. It’s been good to reconnect with the causes I am passionate about. I have been able to spend some time with people that I have known for so long. It is hard to do it from far away.”
Perhaps more so recently because his father, King Charles, has been ill. And on the work front, it hasn’t been easy either.
Six years in the content game offers a case study in how difficult it can be to negotiate the shifting sands of a transformed media landscape, so difficult that even a Hollywood actor and a British prince are not guaranteed to succeed.
Those years have proved there is one bankable aspect of the Sussex brand: their relationship with the royal family continues to be devoured on an industrial scale. However, launching lifestyle brands and philanthropic pursuits that rely purely on name recognition – even with a packed contacts book of A-list friends to help – cannot guarantee reliable success in the cut-throat era of the attention economy.
“The Sussexes have kind of got caught up in the media’s awkward teenage transition,” said Evan Shapiro, a former US media executive turned leading analyst of the creator economy. “Just being famous is no longer enough … The last time Meghan Markle worked in show business [starring in the US legal drama Suits], it was a different era. It was top down: ‘We push it out, you watch it.’ That’s just how it worked.
“That era has passed. It’s fucking hard [now] … the competition is literally every human on earth. Eight billion people with phones who are all competing with Meghan Markle.”
The Sussexes could scarcely have had better timing for their eye-catching 2020 Netflix deal, via their Archewell Productions organisation – global streamers were scrambling for big names to lure subscribers.
The pair were in demand, talking with the likes of Disney and Apple before the Netflix deal was signed. Spotify was also pursuing big-name deals when it secured the Sussexes.
While the Netflix announcement talked of a raft of potential projects, the greatest prize was always the story of the Sussexes’ relationship with the royal family. The subsequent 2022 documentary series, Harry & Meghan, duly delivered, setting record viewing figures for a documentary debut and ranking as one of its most successful docuseries ever.
Other Netflix projects featuring the couple followed, including the Live to Lead interview series, Harry’s Polo documentary and two series of the cooking and lifestyle show With Love, Meghan.
Unsurprisingly, content without the royal intrigue could not hit the heights of Harry & Meghan. Polo failed to make Netflix’s top 10 lists around the world, while ratings for the second series of With Love, Meghan dropped off. It was the 1,217th most watched title on Netflix over the second half of last year. A mooted animated children’s series, Pearl, was cancelled.
Netflix also ended its partnership with Meghan’s lifestyle brand, As Ever, after seven months. The company said handing full control to Meghan was always the plan. However, the relationship endures. Netflix renewed its partnership with the Sussexes, but slimmed it down to a “first look” deal.
As for podcasting, the Spotify deal was ended by mutual consent in 2023, having only produced Meghan’s 12-episode podcast Archetypes, featuring interviews with people such as the former tennis champion Serena Williams and pop star Mariah Carey.
![Meghan stirs a drink in a cocktail glass on a kitchen island while talking to Mindy Kaling](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9afa41960213980602ba460fe0892244f1cfc38e/0_0_3000_2000/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Meghan subsequently launched another podcast series, Confessions of a Female Founder, in 2025, with Lemonada Media. Only nine episodes were made. She revealed last year that there would be no second series, saying she was focusing on As Ever.
In line with all of Harry and Meghan’s exploits, there have been some acerbic assessments of their media production efforts. Most notably, the Spotify executive Bill Simmons called them “fucking grifters” after the company’s deal with the couple ended.
Less incendiary industry analysts point to the significant timing. The Sussexes’ narrowed Netflix deal and split with Spotify coincided with content providers cutting back on their big celebrity bets, and the chaos being wrought by the rapid rise of the creator economy.
“This isn’t a story about nobody being interested in [the Sussexes],” said Matt Navarra, a social media consultant who has worked with broadcasters. “It’s quite the opposite. They can generate attention almost on demand. The harder thing is converting attention into a repeatable media proposition.
“Harry and Meghan arrived in Hollywood with almost every advantage imaginable, but audiences now effectively have infinite choice. They don’t care about how expensive the deal was, or how famous the person is.
“I think that’s one of the brutal lessons of the new media world: that fame can buy you the first click, but only the content earns the second … Their original Harry & Meghan series was pretty much a blockbuster. What they’ve struggled with is repeatability.”
Several industry insiders noted the comparisons with the Obamas, whose Higher Ground production company’s multi-year deal with Netflix narrowed to a “first look” deal in 2024. Their Spotify deal also ended in 2022.
Shapiro said the Sussexes had not yet proved they could draw big audiences beyond content directly related to their dealings with the royal family. “By no fault of their own, the Sussexes were not prepared for the current moment,” he said. “It turns out, other than marrying a prince, Meghan Markle just isn’t that special. Other than being born into royalty, Harry’s just not that interesting.”
Navarra said: “Enormous curiosity exists around them, but curiosity about a person isn’t necessarily the same as demand for everything that person produces. Celebrity is a distribution advantage, but it isn’t a content strategy.
“Harry and Meghan show that you can inherit enormous attention and still have to earn the audience every single time. To me, that is the really interesting shift.”
![Meghan, as Rachel Zane, with Patrick J Adams, as Michael Ross, sitting on a sofa in a living room](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b180be50e1b93d2548263f5d8ef11148344457c9/0_0_3000_2000/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
It is perhaps understandable, then, that Meghan is reportedly returning to a bankable acting career that she put on ice after her marriage to Harry. Initial reports from Australia of a UK-based role for Meghan were backed up by Tina Brown, the former Vanity Fair editor and founding editor of the Daily Beast.
Brown said it had been fuelled by Meghan’s positive experience as a celebrity judge on MasterChef Australia last month. “She finally realised how much easier – and more fun – it is to perform in a hit baked by someone else,” Brown wrote.
“She was back on the market, and it did not take long for Hollywood’s mega-deal machine, WME, the talent agency that still represents her, to get her a role.”
Sources close to the Sussexes have not denied the reports.
On Friday night it was reported that Meghan was in talks to return to acting in Netflix’s series The Gentlemen. According to Variety, she was in discussions to join the third season of the Guy Ritchie-created series.
However, the couple are not out of the media production game. Archewell has evolved into a more traditional production company. Its forthcoming Netflix projects include a polo drama and a film adaptation of the romantic novel Meet Me at the Lake. Several sources familiar with the company said there were also projects in the works beyond Netflix.
In practical terms, the move back to the UK creates few issues for their media ambitions. It is not unusual for major production companies to sit outside Hollywood and make shows away from the US, and the UK remains a major production hub.
As for Harry, he – or anyone else – will struggle to replicate the runaway media success of his memoir, Spare. He is focusing on his Invictus Games coming to Birmingham next year. Meanwhile, Meghan has suggested any return as a business podcaster may depend on the progress of her lifestyle brand.
“I would love to bring the show back when I am at a different end of my founder journey,” she said last summer, explaining why she had put her Confessions of a Female Founder podcast on hold. “I think a different time will be so exciting to compare and contrast.”
summary: Since relocating to California in 2020, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have faced a challenging media landscape, resulting in pared-back or expired mega-deals with companies like Netflix and Spotify. While projects centered on their royal connections achieved massive success, their non-royal content struggled to maintain large audiences. As they prepare to return to the UK, the couple continues to adjust their media strategies, with Meghan reportedly in talks to return to acting.
key_points: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex signed major multi-million-dollar deals with Netflix and Spotify after moving to the US in 2020.
Their 2022 Netflix docuseries about their royal exit broke viewing records, but subsequent non-royal content failed to match that success.
Their Spotify partnership ended in 2023, and their Netflix deal was later narrowed to a 'first look' agreement.
Industry analysts noted that while the couple can easily generate initial attention, converting that fame into repeatable media content has proven difficult.
Meghan Markle is reportedly in talks to return to acting in the third season of Netflix's The Gentlemen.

title: From Booker-listed Marlon James to a memoir by Michael Douglas – the biggest books this autumn
author: Guardian staff reporter
content:
Fiction
The Disappearers by Marlon James
Hamish Hamilton, 3 September
  After a detour into mythic fantasy, the author of the Booker-winning A Brief History of Seven Killings returns to Jamaica. This account of a brutal homophobic attack on a group of gay actors in 1980s Kingston has already been longlisted for this year’s prize.
The Bridge by Colm Tóibín
Picador, 3 September
  Twenty years on, this short novel is a sequel to Tóibín’s exquisite story A Long Winter, set around a family tragedy in the isolated Pyrenees. Now the building of a bridge brings modernity, possibility and threat to a father and son, in a spare chronicle of longing and grief.
![The Golden Hours by Louisa Young](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d3eb1c4e41dbf00c09751edbd6691db086f6ea14/0_0_328_500/master/328.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Golden Hours by Louisa Young
Mantle, 3 September
  Young continues her aunt Elizabeth Jane Howard’s much-loved Cazalet Chronicles, bringing her story of a sprawling upper-middle-class English family into the swinging 60s.
Switzy by Emma Cline
Chatto & Windus, 10 September
  With dementia making him increasingly confused, David is on his way to a clinic in Zurich to end his life while he still has the capacity to make a choice. Longlisted for the Booker prize, this is a bravura portrait of a failing mind, told from the inside.
The Rouse by China Miéville
Picador, 17 September
  A leading light of the New Weird, Miéville has been working on this stonking 1,000-page supernatural fantasy for two decades. Political intrigue, continent-hopping global conspiracy and uncanny mysteries unfold.
![The Housekeeper by Rose Tremain](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a521faa44289f9e3848975b665a50b9253af0daf/0_0_650_1000/master/650.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Housekeeper by Rose Tremain
Chatto & Windus, 17 September
  An origin story for Daphne du Maurier’s enduring bestseller Rebecca is told from the perspective of the novelist’s secret lover Danni, housekeeper in a Cornish mansion, who is outraged to find herself recast on the page as the malevolent Mrs Danvers.
Stations by Louise Kennedy
Bloomsbury, 24 September
  The author of bestselling 2022 debut novel Trespasses, a Troubles-set love story recently adapted into a C4 drama starring Gillian Anderson, returns with a tale of friendship and loss. Róisín and Red meet in small-town Ireland in the 1980s and reconnect in a London squat, before Red is caught up in a cycle of poverty and addiction.
Doom Painting by AK Blakemore
Granta, 24 September
  One of our most exciting historical novelists takes on the peasants’ revolt, in a blow-by-blow account of unlikely leader Wat Tyler and the 16 days in 1381 that turned England upside down. With cinematic action and a relish for medieval vocabulary, it’s a punky successor to Hilary Mantel.
![Barbara Kingsolver, Marlon James, Bonnie Garmus, Jonathan Coe, Yiyun Li and Emma Cline.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6943583990f4f30cf64771d2834c425571368eba/0_0_2953_2362/master/2953.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee
   4th Estate, 29 September
  The hagwon or cram school is a symbol of Korea’s stress on education. This new saga from the Pachinko author follows a middle-class family, their life in ruins after the 1997 Asian financial crisis, who move to Sydney and then California in search of a better future for their children.
![Partita by Barbara Kingsolver](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f692476d5c7a4deb4a5a1f953fa7ea21a7266cb9/0_0_325_500/master/325.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Partita by Barbara Kingsolver
Faber, 6 October
  After the Pulitzer-winning Demon Copperhead, a retelling of David Copperfield set in Appalachia, Kingsolver returns with a quieter tale of midlife longing and regret. A gifted pianist, Livia used music to escape the sadness of her family life in rural Tennessee, but having married and resettled in her home town, an unexpected call from a former lover drags her back into the past.
Life Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger
Jonathan Cape, 13 October
  Set a quarter of a century on, this long-awaited sequel focuses on the daughter of the couple in The Time Traveler’s Wife. Alba has inherited her father’s extraordinary condition, jumping unpredictably across the decades, from a United States in turmoil to a dystopian future London. She’s torn between two lovers – one anchored in the present, and one a time traveller like herself.
Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus
Manilla, 13 October
  In the follow-up to global bestseller Lessons in Chemistry, it’s 1982 New York and young Batter Gray lands a job at the eponymous poetry periodical, run by feuding twin brothers. Expect charm, quirk and literary rabbit holes.
![In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/aa9c8b59d38fbc5ee5aadd7d396c897348f135dd/0_0_654_1000/master/654.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak
Viking, 15 October
  From the Booker and Women’s prize-shortlisted author, a study of French writer Gustave Flaubert refracted through the lives of the women around him, including his most iconic creation: Madame Bovary.
Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li
   4th Estate, 22 October
  Set at the end of the 18th century, against a background of global tumult, the Pulitzer winner’s historical epic is inspired by the lives of two musicians: Adelaide Percheron, born in French India, and the Irish John Field, the inventor of the nocturne, who will be brought together by love and talent.
Lessons in Harmony by Jonathan Coe
Viking, 12 November
  Music is in the air this autumn: Coe’s latest follows the friendship between French dandy Maurice Ravel and English traditionalist Ralph Vaughan Williams, exploring creativity and national identity against the encroaching shadow of the first world war.
Crime and thrillers
Sherlock Holmes, Miss Marple and George Smiley return
![CrimeColumnBooks](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0c9f6a7fccd74b0a5f1ef0b9263c39959ec19904/0_0_2953_2362/master/2953.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Autumn is back-to-school season for series authors, with William Boyd on the third of his cold war espionage novels starring travel writer Gabriel Dax. In Cold Sunset (Viking, 3 September) our reluctant spy is on his way to Russia, to tussle with the KGB. Richard Osman serves up number two in his We Solve Murders franchise: We Chase Shadows (Viking, 10 September) sees Steve, Amy and Rosie – retired cop, private security officer and bestselling crime author respectively – investigate after a body is found in the Italian hills. Five years on, Janice Hallett publishes a sequel to her hit am-dram debut The Appeal, as the Fairway Players’ new production of Agatha Christie leads to murder in The Silent Appeal (Viper, 3 September). The vigorous afterlife of the queen of crime continues elsewhere, with the first official new outing for Miss Marple, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, 22 September). A varied cast list, death on the mountaintop and plenty of suspects are guaranteed.
Ian Rankin, known for his grumpy Edinburgh detective John Rebus, takes a new direction in The Heights (Orion, 8 October), a standalone thriller set in a luxurious central London high-rise. And there’s a return to the world of John le Carré’s Circus in the latest from his son Nick Harkaway: in The Taper Man (Viking, 5 November), George Smiley finds himself navigating the unlikely terrain of 1960s LA in search of a communist sleeper agent.
Finally, a festive treat: 10 new adventures for the world’s most famous detective in short story anthology Sherlock (Simon & Schuster, 5 November), with contributors including Sarah Perry, Joe Hill, Abir Mukherjee and Kate Mosse.
Nonfiction
Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer 
Penguin Michael Joseph, 22 September
  Thirty years after Princess Diana was killed in a car crash, her brother – whose euology at her funeral echoed around the world – tells the story of their upbringing and recounts the devastating week of her death.
The Castle by Jon Ronson 
Viking, 20 August
  A concerning late-night call from his teenage son marks the start of a strange journey into modern masculinity for the journalist and author of The Psychopath Test and So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed.
The Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown
Simon & Schuster, 1 September
  The former PM tries to join the dots between two seemingly disparate political phenomena: the erosion of the international rules-based order, exacerbated by war and climate breakdown, and the fragmentation of the tight-knit communities that keep us connected at a local level.
![The Great Dictator- A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6146e00e5791a57a87d37684bd1af5d43d8b0286/0_0_650_1000/master/650.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet 
Hodder & Stoughton, 10 September
  The queen of romance novels wrote a scarcely believable 723 of them during her career – with a little help from an amanuensis or two. Historian Sweet tells the extraordinary story of a woman born into an upper‑middle-class family fallen on hard times, who navigated scandal and opprobrium to become one of the bestselling writers of the 20th century.
Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History by Lucy Worsley 
Hodder & Stoughton, 3 September 
  The historian and chief curator of royal palaces brings a personal touch to some of British history’s pivotal moments, focusing on the places in which they unfolded, and in which Worsley herself has worked: Hampton Court, Kensington Palace and the Tower of London.
All the Wrong Moves by Anthony Scaramucci 
Bodley Head, 17 September
  Not many political figures are able to give Liz Truss a run for her money in the shortest-ever-tenure stakes, but Scaramucci, Trump’s press secretary for just 10 days, is one of them. Since then he’s reinvented himself as one of the administration’s sharpest critics. His first book is an attempt to chart how the US went from stable postwar consensus to today’s “shitshow politics”.
![End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/36d469ed614e95ebf35f912d81fb225b2bbce37d/0_0_311_500/master/311.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor 
Allen Lane, 15 September
  Thinkers and activists Klein and Taylor have identified a distinctive strand of rightwing nihilism: the kind that seeks to reshape the world in its image, even as it devours the natural resources on which our survival depends (certain tech barons and authoritarian leaders may feel particularly seen). Here they offer both a diagnosis and a plan for resistance.
Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Make a Difference? by Jared Diamond 
Mariner, 22 September
  The author of Guns, Germs and Steel, known for his analyses of the grand, impersonal forces that shape human destiny, returns with a timely book on the role of prominent individuals. What difference does a sports coach, a CEO or an erratic president really make to the fortunes of teams, companies and global civilisation?
An Unexpected Life: A Memoir by Gloria Steinem 
Ebury, 22 September
  A totemic figure in American feminism, Steinem sought to carry the momentum of the civil rights era into what became known as the women’s liberation movement. Here she writes about her childhood and political awakening, and reflects from the present moment on nearly 60 years of activism.
![(Left to right) Joe Biden, Colin Kaepernick, Naomi Klein, Malcolm Gladwell and Judi Dench.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/127920214e53fe6dbe162065caebb3402f4d84c1/0_0_2953_2362/master/2953.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Hawking: His Life and Work by Graham Farmelo
John Murray, 24 September
  In the first authorised biography of Stephen Hawking, Farmelo paints an intimate portrait of the acclaimed physicist based on unique access to his diaries and letters, as well as interviews with family and close associates.
The American Way of Killing: The Invention of an Epidemic by Malcolm Gladwell
Abacus, 29 September
  The author of The Tipping Point asks why the United States has ended up being so much more violent than comparable countries around the world. From a Chicago ER to a 17th-century court case, he explores stories that may hold the key to what he describes as “the most pressing of all American social problems”.
![Blockers- Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/8ea59f705d04f749d86b543d39ba8c5fa2aa46ef/0_0_650_1000/master/650.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis 
Allen Lane, 6 October
  Lewis’s pacy, high-stakes nonfiction has been drawing readers since 1989’s Liar’s Poker, an account of his time on Wall Street in the 1980s. Here he deploys his powers of narration to tell the story of how the US Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) sought to dismantle the state – though his real subject is the principled civil servants who stood in the way of Elon Musk’s campaign of vandalism.
Requiem for Gaza by Joe Sacco and Chris Hedges 
Jonathan Cape, 8 October 
  The master of graphic reportage and author of Palestine teams up with veteran war correspondent Hedges to document the devastating Israeli war on Gaza and its human impact. Interviewing 29 displaced Palestinian families, Sacco and Hedges tell stories of death, destruction and resilience.
The Perilous Fight by Colin Kaepernick
Grand Central Publishing, 8 October
  The NFL quarterback made history in 2016 when he knelt for the US national anthem, rather than standing. Since that time, “taking the knee” has become an emblem of the fight for racial justice, in the US and beyond. In his memoir, Kaepernick traces the relationships and experiences that culminated in a pivotal sporting and political moment.
![Promise Me, America by Joe Biden](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ebce8ea91d21a81b06b674d4ffbd2cb49e58eca9/0_0_265_400/master/265.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Promise Me, America by Joe Biden
John Murray, 17 November
  A year on from 107 Days, in which former vice-president Kamala Harris detailed her boss’s failure to get out of the way, Joe Biden tells his side of the story in a book which promises to reveal “the deeply agonising calculation behind his decision … to step aside from the presidential race”.
Pay Attention by Laura Kuenssberg
Corsair, 5 November 
  The former BBC political editor’s first book reflects on 20 years of upheaval in British politics, and what the broadcaster perceives as being at the root of it all: a failure by the political class to really listen to what people have actually been saying.
Holding Lightning: The Life, Loves and Art of Whitney Houston by Emily Lordi
White Rabbit, 1 October
  English professor Lordi treats the career of one of pop’s greatest stars with the seriousness it deserves, but with emotional intelligence too, tracing the arc of Houston’s life from global success to personal tragedy.
Memoir
From Hollywood hijinks to political scandal – life stories to look out for
![MemoirsColumnBooks](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/bd677922fcab1aa95e8ce6ee874d3ce13fcc6d7f/0_0_2953_2362/master/2953.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
It’s another bumper autumn for Hollywood stars with plenty of tales to tell – though this year skews male. Michael Douglas’s One Helluva Ride (Headline, 6 October) includes details of “affairs with some of the most celebrated actresses in Hollywood” and the “serious drug addiction that threatened to destroy his first marriage and career”. If you’re still in the mood for testosterone-laced hijinks after that, there’s Sylvester Stallone’s The Steps (Seven Dials, 29 September), which charts the Rocky star’s 1970s journey from homelessness to the Oscars. For a more multilayered take on acting and fame, try Fictional Selves by Kyle MacLachlan (Century, 29 September), whose talent in picking idiosyncratic roles such as such as Agent Cooper in Twin Peaks has earned him a cult following. And then there’s screen icon Dustin Hoffman, whose first memoir Look at Me (Gallery, 10 November), published as he prepares to enter his 10th decade, covers the pressures of being dubbed the “voice of a generation” after The Graduate, and his many acting roles since that extraordinary breakthrough. It would make a neat pairing with Watergate reporter Bob Woodward’s memoir Secrets (Simon & Schuster, 24 November): that era-defining scoop was dramatised in All the President’s Men, with Hoffman playing Woodward’s partner, Carl Bernstein.
On the other side of the Atlantic, Judi Dench reminisces about a 70-year career in Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? (Michael Joseph, 22 October). In Vigilauntie (W&N, 3 September) actor and co-creator of the groundbreaking sketch show Goodness Gracious Me, Meera Syal, writes about family, frustration and making it as an Asian woman on TV, while another veteran of the small screen, Russell T Davies, charts a writing career that has spanned Coronation Street and Doctor Who in The Queerest of Folk (Bantam, 8 October). Everyone’s favourite communist standup Alexei Sayle gets political in How I’ve Tried to Change the World (W&N, 3 September), a memoir of protest through the decades, while actual politician and scourge of the BNP in her Barking constituency, Margaret Hodge, shares the lessons of a life on the frontlines in Battle Axe (William Collins, 10 September).
summary: The upcoming autumn publishing season features a diverse array of new fiction, crime thrillers, and nonfiction releases. Notable works include fiction by acclaimed authors like Marlon James, Colm Tóibín, and Min Jin Lee, alongside highly anticipated crime sequels and anthologies. Nonfiction highlights range from Charles Spencer's memoir of Princess Diana to political and historical analyses by prominent writers.
key_points: Several acclaimed novelists return with major new fiction, including Marlon James, Colm Tóibín, and Barbara Kingsolver.
The crime and thriller genre features returning characters such as Sherlock Holmes, Miss Marple, and George Smiley.
Nonfiction releases include Charles Spencer's personal book about his sister, Princess Diana, and memoirs from figures like Gloria Steinem.
Political and historical commentary features heavily in the autumn nonfiction lineup, with works by Gordon Brown, Naomi Klein, and Lucy Worsley.

title: Gillian Anderson on sex, death and saying no to Weinstein
author: Adam White
content:
Every week in the 1990s, Gillian Anderson would throw on a sensible, well-pressed pantsuit and face off against a parade of extraterrestrials and boogeymen. Being a famous woman of the Nineties, Anderson also found herself somewhat inevitably facing off against the era’s IRL boogeymen, such as Harvey Weinstein, the huffing, puffing uber-producer who shaped the film industry back then. He’d always want her to star in “scary things” for him, she once recalled, as if TV’s most prolific monster magnet would want nothing more than to replicate her day job on the big screen, too.
“I mean, he’d try to get me to do his films, period,” Anderson, 58, says today, with the cool, husky drawl of a Wild West gunslinger. She’s famously bidialectal, due to her upbringing between London and Grand Rapids, Michigan, and today is on a video call from France – a neutral ground, maybe, but one she’s chosen to speak with an American accent in. Anyway, she remembers her interactions with Weinstein always involving “a kind of bribery” with an element of quid pro quo. “He’d say, ‘if you do this for me, I’ll do that for you.’ That kind of thing.” She leans her head to her right, before firing off a very Dana Scully-coded roll of the eye. “I didn’t buy into that at all.”
Weinstein is invoked early in Anderson’s new erotic thriller, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, a glowy, sultry celebration of the slasher movie, which also doubles as a bit of a meta commentary on Anderson herself. Playing Billy Presley, a horror icon famed for a starring role in a B-movie film franchise, Anderson tells the prodigious young filmmaker (the actor and comedian Hannah Einbinder, of the acclaimed Hacks) hoping to work with her that she doesn’t scare easily – after all, Billy says, she auditioned for The Burning, a real-life Friday the 13th knock-off that served as Weinstein’s first producer credit.
Anderson’s casting in Camp Miasma is in tribute to writer and director Jane Schoenbrun’s early love of The X-Files. “That show took up probably 50 per cent of my imagination as a kid,” Schoenbrun tells me. “Gillian was always in my life back then, so there was this ephemeral feeling while working with her of having always known them, even though I’d just met them.”
Financiers want to hear a sob story. They always want a minority filmmaker to talk about how their life has been hard, and why they’re dysfunctional
Plus there’s the sex of it all. Camp Miasma is about horror, but it’s also about orgasms. The earliest thoughts of sexual longing felt by Kris, Einbinder’s character, came as she watched archetypal horror heroines flee from masked men – usually while dressed in their underwear, occasionally right before they were horribly butchered. It’s the kind of fantasy that would make Freud’s eye twitch, but also not trouble Anderson in the slightest. She’s about to publish her second collection of erotic fantasies, crowdsourced online. One woman wrote to her about wanting to be tied down by her own dentist; another admitted she craves the sexual freedom that would be instigated by her husband’s demise. In Camp Miasma, it is Billy who grants Kris the freedom to voice, then indulge, those fantasies of hers. It’s as if Anderson took her brilliantly frank sex therapist from Netflix’s Sex Education, drenched her in blood, then sent her overseas to save the world’s libidos one person at a time.
Upon receiving the Camp Miasma script, Anderson began to see the parallels. “It made perfect sense for me to play Billy,” she says, “because of how many layers of the role aligned with what I’ve been talking about quite avidly over the last years.” She gleefully stepped into what she terms “the meta world” of the film. “How bizarre that this would come into my life at this very moment,” she adds. “I felt like I had to do it.”
![Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson in ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/21/15/36/CampMiasma_Still_6_MUBI.jpeg)
It is May, and we’re speaking a few hours before Camp Miasma’s Cannes Film Festival premiere – where it would go on to earn raves, and ultimately take home the event’s Queer Palm award. Next to a glamorously coiffed Anderson is a groggy Einbinder, 31, who is valiantly persevering through a press junket despite being struck down with flu. Like Anderson, she saw herself in Camp Miasma. She identifies as bisexual, with Kris’s “emotional journey” mirroring hers as a young woman. “You start with discomfort, then shame, then liberation,” she says. “I related to it enormously.”
Kris, too, shares parallels with Jane Schoenbrun, who at 39 is the most exciting millennial filmmaker working today. They specialise in work that is spooky and nerdy and lightly otherworldly, rooted in pop culture ephemera and body horror both literal and supernatural. Their commercial breakthrough was 2024’s breathtaking I Saw the TV Glow, about two outcast teenagers drawn together by their shared love of a fictional supernatural drama called The Pink Opaque, which starts to bleed into reality.
Like Schoenbrun and their dysphoric 2021 thriller We’re All Going to the World’s Fair, Kris’s character in Camp Miasma debuted with a tiny independent film that was warmly received at the Sundance Film Festival – a remake of Psycho told from the perspective of the shower curtain. Also like Schoenbrun, who was sought out to direct a reboot of the flagging Leprechaun franchise (the 1993 original saw a terribly bewigged Warwick Davis chase around a pre-fame Jennifer Aniston), Kris is asked to take the reins of the long-dormant Camp Miasma movies (think an even grimier version of the Friday the 13th series). But unlike Schoenbrun, Kris accepts the movie offer, sending her down a rabbit hole with Billy that unlocks her own psychosexual malaise.
![Jane Schoenbrun, Anderson and Einbinder attend the LA premiere of ‘Camp Miasma’ in July](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/21/15/06/GettyImages-2288229038.jpeg)
Making Camp Miasma, Schoenbrun experienced a similar blossoming. They grew up watching horror movies that cast genderqueer or trans characters as sickos and deviants: think Psycho, The Silence of the Lambs, or the fascinatingly offensive Friday the 13th copy-paste Sleepaway Camp. “I knew that if I was to develop a more positive relationship to sex and to my own body, I had to return to those Buffalo Bills or Norman Bateses, who I loved as a young person but who also probably f***ed me up.”
Today, Schoenbrun stands alone in the Hollywood ecosystem, as the only out trans filmmaker commanding high budgets (relatively speaking, anyway) and major studio backing. It’s no exaggeration – even with The Matrix and Bound as her calling cards, Lilly Wachowski said this month that no one is willing to fund her $10m new indie. It’s a fact that Schoenbrun finds daunting. “The thing I’ve learnt is that financiers want to hear a sob story,” they explain. “They always want a minority filmmaker to talk about how their life has been hard, and why they’re dysfunctional.”
You basically have to fake it until you make it, Schoenbrun explains. “I’ve kind of mastered the language of the pitch meeting. I wouldn’t be sitting here if I hadn’t.” So in those rooms selling Camp Miasma, they leant into the critical acclaim they’d received for TV Glow, the fact that they’re a Sundance Film Festival fave, and that general audiences would love the big, attention-hogging idea of Gillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder as lovers covered in blood. “It’s a process of making your work understandable to the world of capital, and that’s a very different process to actually making the thing,” they say. “They’re not going to care that much about gender transgression in the history of the horror film…”
![Ian Foreman in Jane Schoenbrun’s star-making 2024 movie ‘I Saw the TV Glow’](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/21/15/45/TV-GLOW_04.jpeg)
It explains why Camp Miasma is two films in one – the first is an easier-to-sell slasher satire with severed heads and impalings, the second is a tender, sexy love story flush with queer existentialism. Schoenbrun Trojan-horses us, essentially. “It’s a story of queer liberation,” they say, directly inspired by their own gender journey. I Saw the TV Glow was conceived in a period of trauma at the very beginning of their transition, which explains its occasional fatalism. Camp Miasma, comparatively, is the product of a period of joy. “I often compare transition to getting on an antidepressant,” they joke. “You deal with all of the s****y side effects first, and it takes a couple months before the good stuff starts. This movie was made from a place of full enjoyment with the good stuff – the joy, sex and euphoria of becoming myself.”
Schoenbrun cast Anderson because of The X-Files, and Einbinder because of the physicality she saw in her stand-up specials (“she commits her whole body to performance and not only performance but, like, weird performance”). But there’s also a cool, understated muscle to both actors that makes them evenly matched on-screen, as evidenced by Anderson’s run of steely, impervious women (she’s played everything from Margaret Thatcher in The Crown to A Streetcar Named Desire’s Blanche DuBois at the Young Vic), and in Einbinder’s off-camera activism. Einbinder is currently one of the most high-profile Jewish anti-Zionists working in Hollywood, with her continued advocacy for Palestine – as well as her leftist politics generally – earning her repeated drubbings from conservatives. She says that the industry is set up in a way that makes it consistently difficult to navigate ethically.
![Anderson and Einbinder in ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/21/15/20/CampMiasma_Still_5_MUBI.jpeg)
“Life under capitalism implicates an individual in systems that are evil,” Einbinder says. “End of story, you know what I mean? It’s something that torments me on a daily basis.” How does she get through it? “The way I make sense of it is just to continue to act in a way that is in line with my morals. So I do speak to those things and put action behind them. But it’s not straightforward, and it does eat me up.”
For Anderson, she doesn’t think her own story has involved any real fighting, even when I suggest it probably wasn’t easy to use her X-Files clout to make something like her dazzling adaptation of Edith Wharton’s The House of Mirth, and not whatever Weinstein had in mind for her.
“I’ve never allowed anyone to force me into anything that I didn’t want to do,” she says. “It’s more been about choosing to step away for a period of time, or do theatre, or do an indie film, as opposed to whatever your trajectory is meant to be.” As she says this though, she starts to have second thoughts... “It’s funny, only sometimes in retrospect does one realise there might have been a divine plan all along. I think I’ve always stayed on a path that makes sense for me at any given time. And ultimately you get to a point where you feel like, yes – this does represent who I am.”
“This”, at the moment at least, being Camp Miasma – a bloody, profound and sapphic love story soaked in weirdness and joy. It just feels right that Dana Scully found a home there, doesn’t it?
‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ is in cinemas
summary: Gillian Anderson stars alongside Hannah Einbinder in the erotic slasher thriller "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma," directed by Jane Schoenbrun. The film explores themes of horror, sexual liberation, and queer existentialism, paralleling aspects of the actors' and director's real lives. Anderson reflects on her past encounters with Harvey Weinstein, noting she consistently refused his quid pro quo advances and chose her own career path.
key_points: Gillian Anderson stars as horror icon Billy Presley in Jane Schoenbrun's erotic thriller "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma."
Anderson recounted that her past interactions with Harvey Weinstein involved bribery and quid pro quo attempts, which she firmly rejected.
Director Jane Schoenbrun conceived the film as a story of queer liberation and a joyful exploration of gender transition.
Hannah Einbinder stars alongside Anderson, drawing parallels between her own bisexual journey and her character's emotional arc.

title: FND: I was being treated for dehydration - when suddenly I couldn't move
author: Elaine McGee
content:
![Carmel is looking at the camera and is leaning against her hand. She is in a hospital setting and wires and tubes can be seen beside her. She is wearing a red top with white stripes and has short grey hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/0484/live/a5b39820-9d49-11f1-a3dc-c3f8cfe34ff8.jpg)
Carmel McConnellogue said she could not speak or feel her face and "everything was numb"
- Published
Carmel McConnellogue was in hospital, being treated by medical staff for dehydration, when she suddenly felt she could no longer move her body.
She said she could not speak or feel her face and "everything was numb".
Initial symptoms suggested McConnellogue might have had a stroke - but an MRI scan confirmed that she had Functional Neurological Disorder (FND), meaning there was was a problem with how her brain received and sent information to the rest of her body.
She said she never expected to be diagnosed with a condition she had never heard of.
"I could not believe it," she told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.
"It was explained to me by a doctor that your brain is perfect but it's like a computer and it has too many tabs open.
"My brain went offline, and the body crashed."
McConnellogue, who was being treated at Altnagelvin Hospital in County Londonderry, was told that the condition was brought on by stress and trauma.
"I felt paralysed, trapped and I couldn't stop thinking â I can't move, what is going to happen to me?"
What is FND?
FND is estimated to affect 50,000-100,000 people in the UK.
It limits the brain and nervous system's ability to send and receive signals., external
Its underlying cause is not known, but some experts think it could be linked to stress, trauma or a response to a virus or other inflammatory condition.
Symptoms can vary from person to person, but can include limb weakness, paralysis, seizures, walking difficulties, spasms, sensory issues and cognitive problems.
Some people may experience short-lived symptoms, while other can have them for many years.
Most treatment options come in the form of rehabilitation therapy, according to NHS Inform.
This can include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, and psychological therapy.
![A woman using a zimmer frame to walk. She is wearing a navy vest top and has short grey hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/c230/live/d1dcfbd0-9d49-11f1-813f-d5ac18465183.jpg)
McConnellogue was told that the condition was brought on by stress and trauma
McConnellogue had no power in the left side of her body, and her speech was seriously impacted.
In the initial stages, she could not lift her legs or wiggle her toes.
She stayed in hospital for five weeks while therapists helped her regain her ability to move independently.
The road to recovery has been challenging for the life-long Derry City supporter.
Before her diagnosis, McConnellogue described herself as a "non-stop Duracell bunny, on the go 24/7".
"The physical part is very tough; I walk with a zimmer frame or a crutch and I have to be helped up the stairs, my husband has to physically put me to bed," she added.
She said the diagnosis had "floored" her and she had relied on counselling services to keep her going.
"My independence is gone. I cannot drive, I can't go to the shop on my own - all those things I took for granted," she said.
Country music singer Lisa McHugh spoke publicly last year about being diagnosed with FND.
According to the NHS, there is no cure for FND but it is treatable providing you adapt your life as much as possible to manage it.
McConnellogue has been sharing her recovery journey on social media.
"I do believe FND is misunderstood and I want people to know they are not alone," she said.
"It is a very real neurological condition, and I want to show others you can recover."
'Postcode lottery'
![A woman wearing a pink top looking at the camera. She is wearing a gold necklace and green glasses. She has red hair and earrings. There are red curtains behind her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a62f/live/0a6a36b0-9d55-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Helen Dickson was diagnosed with FND in 2022
FND Matters NI is the only FND charity in Northern Ireland.
The charity estimates there around 5,000 people living with FND in Northern Ireland but they have struggled to obtain specific figures as Northern Ireland's health trusts do not record FND as a primary condition.
Trustee Helen Dickson was diagnosed with the condition in 2022.
"Treatment for FND can be a postcode lottery," she said.
"More awareness and changes in attitudes are needed, and we need FND specific services.
"There can be a misconception that FND symptoms are imagined or 'all in someone's head' but it's very real."
She said healthcare professionals have asked the charity for advice.
![A woman smiling with her hands int he air wearing a red and white zipped up jacket. She has glasses and short brown hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/58b1/live/0bd97f20-9d4a-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
McConnellogue is a supporter of Derry City Football Club
The Department of Health has previously said in response to a question put forward at Stormont that precise numbers of patients with a diagnosis of FND are not currently captured due to limitations in coding and data systems.
The department estimates there are several thousand people in Northern Ireland with FND.
For Carmel McConnellogue, her next recovery goal is to be able to go to watch a football game.
"I am working towards being at Derry City's next home game, I have come through a lot in life and I will overcome FND," she vowed.
"I know my brain computer is going to come back online, and I will be at the Brandywell again."
summary: While being treated for dehydration in a hospital, Carmel McConnellogue suddenly lost the ability to move and speak, with initial symptoms pointing toward a stroke. An MRI confirmed she had Functional Neurological Disorder (FND), a condition where the brain struggles to properly send and receive signals. McConnellogue spent five weeks in the hospital undergoing rehabilitation and now relies on a zimmer frame and assistance from her husband. She is sharing her journey to raise awareness and hopes to overcome the condition.
key_points: Carmel McConnellogue was diagnosed with Functional Neurological Disorder (FND) after suddenly losing movement and speech while hospitalized for dehydration.
FND is a real neurological condition that affects how the brain sends and receives signals, often compared to a computer with too many tabs open.
McConnellogue spent five weeks in the hospital and now requires mobility aids and assistance from her husband for daily tasks.
There is no cure for FND, but it can be treated through rehabilitation therapies and lifestyle adaptations.
Charities and patients in Northern Ireland highlight that FND treatment is a postcode lottery and that health trusts do not record FND as a primary condition.

title: Gillian Anderson wants you to have good sex – and her new film could help
author: Tori Brazier
content:
![This image released by Mubi shows Gillian Anderson, left, and Hannah Einbinder in a scene from "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442454-bcb4-e1787130307671.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Gillian Anderson is stepping into brand new territory with her latest film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, marking her first foray into horror.
And it’s far from your bog-standard fright flick, as a tongue-in-cheek homage to slashers combined with a bracingly bold take on female sexuality.
Just seconds in, there’s a fountain of vibrantly crimson blood shooting several feet in the air after a body is stabbed in a murderous frenzy.
‘It does, it feels that way,’ Anderson – who we’ve seen play roles as varied as Margaret Thatcher, a sex therapist and, of course, FBI Special Agent Dana Scully in The X-Files – tells Metro of her new direction with the movie.
‘It feels new and unique but I’m very proud of it, and proud to be a part of it. I just can’t wait for it to properly come out because I think people are really going to like it.’
Many already have since Cannes Film Festival in May, where it premiered, with five-star review raves from critics for the film dubbed a ‘bizarre pop-cultural black mass of fiercely believed-in trash and kink’ and a ‘Miasma-sterpiece’.
From I Saw the TV Glow’s Jane Schoenbrun, Camp Miasma’s premise sees intellectual young filmmaker Kris (Hannah Einbinder) hired to direct a rebooted instalment of a previously popular but now problematic ‘80s slasher franchise.
After becoming obsessed with casting the reclusive actress who played the original ‘final girl’ in the first film (Anderson) – and after tracking her down to the abandoned campground where the series used to film, and where she now lives – the two descend into sexual and psychological chaos together.
It won the Queer Palm and has steadily been building word of mouth buzz before reaching British shores this week.
‘When we were making it, we were really excited about the stuff we were getting and how it was looking and feeling. So to see that recognised feels really validating,’ shares Einbinder of the meta-slasher film’s reception so far.
But Camp Miasma isn’t just about gory spurting blood (although they both end up covered in it) and murder (although there is a lot of that), it’s also a lot about sex – and specifically women learning to revel in the pleasure of it.
![This image released by Mubi shows Hannah Einbinder in a scene from "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442311-6dfb.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
![This image released by Mubi shows a scene from "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442841-c267.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
This is a familiar topic for Anderson, who edited a collection of anonymous female sexual fantasies – including one of her own – for 2024 bestseller Want, with an ‘even more daring’ follow-up, fittingly titled More, being published next month. But pushing against the more squeamish boundaries placed on female sexuality and how it’s usually depicted isn’t why she signed up for the film, although she understands the surface-level connection.
‘I guess given that I’ve spent the last couple of years talking about fantasy and women’s sexuality and pleasure, it made a lot of sense as to why I would do it or be the one that was asked to do it. It felt ‘of a piece’,’ she accepts.
Camp Miasma’s focus on sex and death together, two things so intrinsically linked in slasher films, is something that Schoenbrun heavily leans into, calling the franchise’s ghostly recurring villain who lurks at the bottom of the lake ‘Little Death’. Meanwhile, Kris reveals that she can only shoot for an orgasm if she fantasises that she’s the sexualised ‘final girl’, a kink she developed from a formative childhood attachment to the first film starring Anderson’s Billy Presley – and which Billy suggests they explore together.
‘I think it’s important, what Jane is saying through this film. I know they [Schoenbrun] talk light-heartedly about just wanting it to lead to people having good sex – which of course is true and great! – but it’s so much deeper than that,’ adds Anderson. ‘And the depth and the narrative feels similar to what I hear from women through the book and conversations that I’ve had around it, in terms of women and sexuality and pleasure, and the complexities and shame.’
![Still from Mubi film Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma Starring Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson Unit Day 04: A Bad Day At Camp Tivoli](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308319978-404e.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Anderson and Einbinder share a very vulnerable and raw connection onscreen, which becomes at points almost mortifying to watch in its intimacy, as if the audience is intruding on something not meant for public consumption. But the actresses are both ten toes down with this, as the kids say.
‘It’s hard to build chemistry. I think you just have it or you don’t,’ says Einbinder. ‘Gillian and I also did such extensive preparation that when we came to start rehearsing the scenes, we both had a lot to offer. We had in-depth conversations about why we were doing what we were doing, and how we were doing it and why it was important for it to feel a certain way.’
Anderson also points out that, as there’s so much of the film that is ‘outside of the realms of reality’ in its meta murderous fantasy scenes, the elements of human intimacy ‘needed to feel as real and intimate as possible in order to balance out the rest of it’.
‘It felt important to get that aspect of it right. But it’s also a bit of a breath of relief, in a sense. Human relief, somehow,’ she adds.
Anderson makes a memorable entrance as glamorous faded star Billy, speaking with a Dolly Parton-esque drawl and exuding Sunset Boulevard vibes. I haven’t read a single review that doesn’t compare her to Norma Desmond.
‘I was trying to steer her away from Sunset Boulevard because that felt too obvious, almost – and I know that we made a choice of a turban at one point,’ admits Anderson. ‘But the accent was important to me from early on. That was a real gateway into her, it felt like it tied me to ‘final girl’ vibes in a way because the particular Southern [accent] has a lot of strength but a lot of vulnerability in it.’
![This image released by Mubi shows Gillian Anderson in a scene from "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442273-8bd6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
![This image released by Mubi shows Hannah Einbinder, left, and Gillian Anderson from the film "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442186-9369.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
But she speaks about ‘piecing together’ Billy in an extremely open and collaborative approach that also understands restrictions like budget. There’s no sense of Anderson’s bursting portfolio or awards pedigree (an Emmy and two Golden Globes, among others) giving her an attitude that she’s got this acting malarkey figured out enough to simply punch in and punch out every time.
‘Sometimes one has an idea in one’s head of what the personality is, what the wardrobe might be, all these different things – and then you show up and you are introduced to a wardrobe person, and they can only get what they can get.’
Anderson suggested the dramatic Twiggy-inspired eye make-up, while Schoenbrun prompted Billy’s deep, back-of-the-throat cackle, which the actress ably (and slightly alarmingly) demonstrates again.
‘That says so much about who she is and her spirit and her personality, and not in a million years would I imagine that she might have done that!’ laughs Anderson. ‘But the fact that, all of a sudden, that was entered into the collection of character traits takes you on a whole other journey in terms of her.’
Anderson is also working alongside Einbinder, who – despite her own Emmy success with hit comedy series Hacks – is remarkably only taking on her second-ever acting role here, after the HBO show, having previously worked as a stand-up comic.
![This image released by Mubi shows Hannah Einbinder in a scene from "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442253-f210.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Einbinder, quick to giggle at her co-star and quietly deferential as they sit together, learned a lot about character work from her.
‘Gillian has such a clear process. She wants to really understand her physical choreography and motivations. Just watching her craft Billy, I feel it gave me permission to really dive into wanting Kris to feel even more real and to make distinct choices,’ Einbinder recalls. ‘Approaching this was so different because Ava in Hacks and I have more crossover, especially in her physical affect, so this was definitely a new process for me to just really, really feel unlike my actual self.’
- 
	![Jacob Elordi as Hig and Jasper in 20th Century Studios' THE DOG STARS. Photo by Fabio Lovino. ?? 2026 20th Century Studios. All Rights Reserved (Picture: Fabio Lovino)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309021192-0ff4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=493px%2C396px%2C1621px%2C913px&resize=646%2C363)
- Holly Willoughby just wants to see 'normal fannies' in porn
- BBC DJ Trevor Nelson reveals brain tumour diagnosis in update after stepping down
- Pop singer dies aged 30 after freak accident in bathroom
This year has been a stellar one for horror, with Einbinder acknowledging an even more appreciative public appetite for it, thanks to the huge success of Backrooms and Obsession.
Cannes also gave a major platform to The Substance the year prior to Camp Miasma, and it ended up a five-time Oscar nominee. Anderson brings up Get Out too, when we discuss the genre’s resurgence and the sense of a shift in the industry towards taking it more seriously as well.
‘I do absolutely feel that way,’ says Einbinder, before adding with a laugh: ‘Hopefully we’re contributing!’
Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma releases in UK cinemas on Friday, August 21.
![Film](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Film-Chris-Hemsworth-448b.png?quality=90&strip=true)
summary: Gillian Anderson stars alongside Hannah Einbinder in Jane Schoenbrun's new meta-slasher horror film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. The movie combines a tongue-in-cheek homage to '80s horror franchises with a bold exploration of female sexuality, pleasure, and the complexities of shame. After premiering and receiving critical acclaim at the Cannes Film Festival, where it won the Queer Palm, the film is set for its UK theatrical release.
key_points: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma marks Gillian Anderson's first foray into the horror genre.
The meta-slasher film was directed by Jane Schoenbrun and co-stars Hannah Einbinder.
The movie explores the intersection of sex and death while focusing on women learning to revel in sexual pleasure.
The film received rave reviews and won the Queer Palm following its premiere at the Cannes Film Festival.

title: Brandon Flowers Goes Country But Gets a Little Lost on the Back Roads
author: Jon Dolan
content:
![Brandon Flowers](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
Ever since Bob Dylan cut Nashville Skyline in 1969, rockers have been going to Music City to refresh their sounds, kick it with the world’s best session pros, and drink deep the rejuvenating well of local realness. For his third solo album, Killers frontman Brandon Flowers has gone all-in with a full-fledged country record. He says the music harkens back to his Utah youth listening to Waylon Jennings and Johnny Cash (music his dad called “country Western”), and he’s hired some A-list hands to help out, including guitarist David Rawlings — who’s made excellent records alongside Gillian Welch — and octogenarian harmonica great Charlie McCoy, who literally played on Nashville Skyline. As a neo-New Wave guy with a heartland jones and drama-king chops, Flowers isn’t bad cosplaying his heroes, even if his brawny rock-opera vocal approach is a bit short on the conversational warmth that makes for truly memorable country singing.
As with the Killers, he blasts away as over-the-top as ever, drunk on sweeping Americana imagery and marveling at the sound of his voice booming across those sweet Nashville studios. He tries his luck with some rollicking cosmic philosophizing on “Does It Ever Cross Your Mind” and “One of Us,” and it more or less works. Backed by strings, spacious twang, and mariachi horns, the sweet highlight “Red Ground” beautifully argues for a more traditionally economic notion of his historical reenactment. And he flips back into straight-up rock on “Tiger’s Blood,” a gentle vignette about life in a Podunk town that turns into a big, hungry-hearted Killers-style anthem.
But the mystery train starts veering off the rails as Flowers wanders away from enjoyable rhinestone reinvention and defaults to the heavy-handed Springsteenian realism that’s sometimes been both his Rosetta stone and his Achilles’ heel. On “Miss America” he plays a rural beauty aging into her harsh consignment in the methy underbelly of the American mythscape — “You used to call me Miss America/ Before you got hooked on speed.” On the wind-swept epic “Angel” we’re gifted wisdom along the lines of “Some fit the mold like a book on a shelf/Some are hard-wired for something else.” He officially loses the plot on the closer, “An American Dream,” wandering the lonely lost highway piling up clichéd rambling-man reckonings until he bumps into Elvis himself, driving a Tesla Model X for some reason. “He laughed when I asked him if it was all worth it/And he cried when he asked me about Lisa Marie.” And there’s the issue: These songs aren’t quite strong enough to be this epically melodramatic, but they’re not self-aware enough to be as funny as you hope they might be.
summary: The Killers frontman Brandon Flowers ventures into country music for his third solo album, collaborating with notable session musicians like David Rawlings and Charlie McCoy. While tracks like "Red Ground" and "Tiger's Blood" showcase strong moments, the album ultimately falters when it leans too heavily into melodrama and heavy-handed realism. As it progresses, the record loses its direction with clichéd lyrics and bizarre narratives, lacking both the strength to be truly epic and the self-awareness to be funny.
key_points: Brandon Flowers released a full-fledged country solo album inspired by his Utah youth and artists like Waylon Jennings and Johnny Cash.
The album features contributions from A-list musicians, including guitarist David Rawlings and harmonica player Charlie McCoy.
Highlights include the sweet track "Red Ground" and the rock-infused "Tiger's Blood."
The record struggles when Flowers relies on heavy-handed Springsteenian realism and over-the-top melodrama.
The album's closer features an eccentric narrative encounter with Elvis driving a Tesla Model X.

title: Jimmy Cricket’s Catholic priest son jokes at funeral it’s ‘not the first time I’ve see him die’
author: Casey Cooper-Fiske; Press Association Senior Entertainment Reporter
content:
Comedian Jimmy Cricket’s son has joked it “isn’t the first time I’ve seen him die” as he led his funeral service.
The joke came as his funeral requiem mass began at Salford Cathedral on Friday, following the Northern Irish comic, born James Mulgrew’s death on August 3 at the age of 80 following his battle with a short illness.
The ceremony was attended by comedy veterans such as Syd Little, Tommy Cannon and Roy Walker and led by Cricket’s youngest son Father Frankie Mulgrew, who once worked as his road manager but is now a Catholic priest.
During the service Father Frankie said: “I just want to say this, this isn’t the first time I’ve seen him die, and rise again, comedy metaphor, it’s a comedy metaphor.
![Roy Walker arrives for the funeral of stand-up comedian Jimmy Cricket](https://www.irishnews.com/resizer/v2/QQIGMCAYNNNRTOWF2GJ5L7L4JQ.jpg?auth=67c11d171b098693eac350923d9490d170171f17ede21f5642f4ae7296715a04&width=800&height=1200)
“Friends, about 20 years ago, my dad said, ‘I will sacrifice grandchildren, you go into the priesthood’.”
Cookstown born Cricket, who was known for his signature bowler hat and catchphrase “And there’s more”, became a TV staple in the 80s, appearing in programmes such as The Good Old Days as well as the Royal Variety Performance.
![Tommy Cannon arrives for the funeral of stand-up comedian Jimmy Cricket](https://www.irishnews.com/resizer/v2/EQ5ECB46T5J7NDMDA6WQI4YNY4.jpg?auth=f6f7e74b6a278db205a34da2aa8e78ac30a8fdc42d2d13f906bc2c14a3b1572c&width=800&height=1147)
The star left school at 16 and spent his summers working as Redcoat camp host at Butlins holiday camps.
He went on to work the comedy club scene throughout the 1970s and 1980s, going on to win LWT’s Search For A Star talent contest before getting his own ITV show, And There’s More, which ran for four seasons.
He later fronted his own programme on BBC Radio 2 before appearing on the Royal Variety Show in the 80s and performing in a number of pantomimes.
summary: Comedian Jimmy Cricket's funeral took place at Salford Cathedral following his death at the age of 80. The service was led by his youngest son, Catholic priest Father Frankie Mulgrew, who humorously remarked during the mass about seeing his father 'die and rise again' as a comedy metaphor. The funeral was attended by numerous comedy veterans, celebrating the life of the Northern Irish comic known for his signature bowler hat and catchphrase.
key_points: Comedian Jimmy Cricket died at age 80 following a short illness.
His funeral requiem mass was held at Salford Cathedral and led by his son, Father Frankie Mulgrew.
Father Frankie joked during the service that it was not the first time he had seen his father 'die' in a comedy metaphor.
Comedy veterans including Syd Little, Tommy Cannon, and Roy Walker attended the ceremony.
Jimmy Cricket was a prominent TV and comedy star in the 1970s and 1980s, known for his signature bowler hat and catchphrase.

title: Edward Bluemel Is Agatha Christie’s Hercule Poirot in BBC, BritBox First-Look Image for ‘Hercule’
author: Georg Szalai
content:
![](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-hollywoodreporter-2021/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
![Edward Bluemel as a young Hercule Poirot in 'Hercule'](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Hercule-Mammoth-Screen-H-2026.jpg?w=2000&h=1126&crop=1) 
Hercule Poirot is here. Well, not quite yet — but a first look at him is.
The BBC and BritBox revealed first-look images of Edward Bluemel (My Lady Jane, Killing Eve, Sex Education, A Discovery of Witches) as a young Hercule Poirot in the upcoming six-part series Hercule from Mammoth Screen and Agatha Christie Ltd. on Friday. Check them out in the main image of this article and a shot from a bit more of a distance below.
The series, which has started filming in Liverpool, is described as “an intimate study of Hercule Poirot, the man, and an epic portrait of Britain between the wars.” Hercule will center around three of Christie’s early stories of the Belgian detective, while also introducing the famous sleuth to future friends and allies and, according to a synopsis, “one particular nemesis …”
Related Stories
![Prince Harry arrives at court on Jan. 21.](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-hollywoodreporter-2021/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
![Prince Harry and Meghan Markle](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-hollywoodreporter-2021/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
Previously unveiled to join Bluemel in the cast of the new series were Henry Ashton (A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, A Good Girl’s Guide to Murder), James D’Arcy (Oppenheimer, Constellations), Calvin Demba (Supacell, Life), Phil Dunning (Smoggie Queens, Am I Being Unreasonable?), Jack Gleeson (House of Guinness, In the Land of the Saints and Sinners), Tamsin Greig (Riot Women, Friday Night Dinner), James Nesbitt (Cold Feet, Run Away), Guy Remmers (The Buccaneers, Lessons), Rebecca Rittenhouse (His & Hers, Maggie) and Mawaan Rizwan (Juice, The Split Up).
Christie’s Poirot novels have sold more than 750 million copies. Hercule is produced by Mammoth Screen, part of ITV Studios, and Agatha Christie Ltd. for BBC iPlayer and BBC One in the U.K., as well as BritBox in North America in 2027.
Written by Benji Walters (Code of Silence, The Leopard, Obsession), the first two episodes are being directed by Jonny Campbell (Am I Being Unreasonable?, In the Flesh), with Chanya Button (Code of Silence, Doctor Who) and Alrick Riley (Bridgerton, How to Get Away With Murder) directing the middle two and final two episodes, respectively. Charlie Palmer (A Woman of Substance, Extraordinary) serves as series producer.
![](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-hollywoodreporter-2021/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
The executive producers are Walters and Campbell, James Prichard for Agatha Christie Ltd., Rebecca Durbin and Damien Timmer for Mammoth Screen, Nick Lambon for the BBC and Robert Schildhouse, Jon Farrar and Stephen Nye for BritBox.
Fifth Season is handling global distribution for Hercule.
